title: Track 1, Lesson 5: The emergency fund - a cushion against every shock
subtitle: Without an emergency fund, a small shock (job loss, illness) can push you into a spiral of debt.
whyItMatters: An emergency fund is why one person who suddenly loses their job still sleeps well, while another is borrowing at punishing rates after a single month without pay. This lesson helps you work out the right amount and where to keep it.
openingQuestion: Where should you keep an emergency fund so it is both safe and available the moment you need it?
openingOptions: Buy physical gold and keep it at home, secure against everything
A savings account you can draw on within 1-2 days
Lend it to friends, to earn well above a bank deposit rate
Put the whole reserve in shares, so it grows while you wait
explanation: The purpose of an emergency fund is SAFETY and LIQUIDITY (getting it out quickly when needed), not a high return. Shares can fall in value at exactly the moment you urgently need the money (the market dropping just as you lose your job) - a risk not worth taking with a fund whose whole purpose is protection.

diagram.label: Falling into a spiral of debt

realWorldExample.description: Someone with six months of spending in an emergency fund can lose their job suddenly and still look calmly for the right next role; someone without one usually has to take the first job they find however low the pay, or borrow at very high rates just to keep going.

quiz.question: How many months of essential spending should a standard emergency fund cover?
options: 24 months, for complete peace of mind against any possible shock
1-2 months, enough to get through to the next payday
3-6 months, or 6-12 months if your income is irregular
Exactly three months of income, rather than of spending
quiz.explanation: Three to six months of essential spending is the common standard for someone with stable income (a full-time employee). People with irregular income (freelancers, the self-employed) should hold 6-12 months, because the risk of an interruption is higher.

quiz.question: Why not keep the whole emergency fund in shares, even though the expected return beats a savings account?
options: Because shares take at least 30 days to sell
Because using shares as an emergency fund is prohibited by law
Because share returns are always lower than a savings account pays
Because shares can fall exactly when you need to withdraw urgently
quiz.explanation: The biggest risk is bad correlation in timing: an economic crisis usually pushes the whole market down AND unemployment up at the same time - so at the moment you need the money most, the asset is worth least. That is why an emergency fund belongs somewhere stable, not somewhere high-returning.

quiz.question: Your essential spending is 12 million a month and your income from your employer is stable. Roughly how large should your emergency fund be?
options: 36-72 million (3-6 months of spending)
12-24 million (only 1-2 months of spending)
120-240 million (10-20 months of spending)
6-12 million (half a month)
quiz.explanation: With stable income from an employer, the 3-6 month standard fits: 12m × 3 = 36m at the minimum, up to 12m × 6 = 72m for more comfort. Twelve months is unnecessary unless income is unstable or you work in an industry with a high risk of layoffs.

quiz.question: Essential spending of 10 million a month, and you freelance so income is irregular. What is the target?
options: 30-60 million (= 10 × 3 to 6, the level for stable income)
60-120 million (= 10 million × 6 to 12 months of essentials)
120 million (= 10 × 12, the ceiling that applies to everybody)
10 million (= exactly one month of essential spending is enough)
quiz.explanation: With irregular income the gap between two contracts is longer and harder to predict, so the standard is 6-12 months rather than 3-6: 10 × 6 = 60 million up to 10 × 12 = 120 million. The 3-6 month range is for people on a fixed monthly salary.

quiz.question: Which is the most suitable place to hold an emergency fund?
options: A 24-month term deposit, since the rate beats shorter terms
An equity fund, so the money is not eroded by inflation over time
A short-term deposit or an instantly accessible account
Gold bars, since gold holds its value well in an economic crisis
quiz.explanation: The two criteria are safety and liquidity, not yield. Breaking a 24-month deposit early costs nearly all the interest; gold and shares can both be falling exactly when you need the money - and income shocks tend to arrive alongside bad markets.

keyTakeaways: Emergency fund = 3-6 months of essential spending (6-12 if income is irregular), held somewhere you can draw on within 1-2 days
The purpose is safety and liquidity, not a high return - this fund should not be invested in shares
Without an emergency fund, a small shock turns into a spiral of debt very easily

practicePrompt.question: You have 60 million in an emergency fund sitting in a low-interest instant-access account. A friend suggests moving it all into blue-chip shares so 'the money isn't idle', since you rarely need it anyway. Is that good advice?
options: No - the purpose of an emergency fund is safety and liquidity, not a high return
Yes, because blue-chip shares are always exactly as liquid and as safe as money held on deposit at a bank
Yes, because the higher the return on an emergency fund the better, and liquidity stops mattering if you rarely draw on it
It makes no difference, because an emergency fund only has to exist in some asset form, with no need to consider liquidity
practicePrompt.explanation: The purpose of an emergency fund is safety and liquidity, not a high return - investing it in shares can force you to sell at a loss exactly when you most urgently need the cash.

summary.keyIdea: Emergency fund = 3-6 months of essential spending (6-12 if income is irregular), accessible within 1-2 days
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: The purpose is safety and liquidity, not a high return - this fund should not be invested in shares

application.title: Work it out now
application.message: Take your monthly essential spending and multiply by 3 to 6 - that is the emergency fund you should have. Compare it with what you actually hold today.
application.secondary: If it falls short, don't worry - knowing the gap is the most important step.

sections.text: A small shock - losing a job, sudden illness, the bike breaking down - should not be the start of a spiral of debt. An emergency fund is the cushion that stops it: money set aside, always available, never used for anything but a genuine emergency.
The purpose is safety, not return

An emergency fund exists for two reasons: SAFETY (it doesn't lose value exactly when you need it) and LIQUIDITY (you can get it out within a day or two). So even though shares carry a higher expected return than a savings account, this is not where an emergency fund belongs - the biggest risk is bad correlation in timing: an economic crisis usually drives the market down AND unemployment up together. At the moment you lose your job and need money most, shares are worth least, and you are forced to sell at a loss.

The common standard is 3-6 months of essential spending for someone with stable income (a full-time employee). People with irregular income - freelancers, the self-employed - should raise it to 6-12 months, because the risk of an interruption is far higher. **Example:** essential spending of 12 million a month with stable employment puts the emergency fund somewhere between 36 and 72 million (12 million × 3 up to 12 million × 6).

items: Keep it somewhere you can draw on quickly: an instant-access savings account, or a short deposit that is easy to break
Don't invest an emergency fund in shares, however much higher the expected return
Freelancers and anyone with unstable income: raise the standard to 6-12 months rather than 3-6
Build the emergency fund first, and only then consider riskier investing - the order matters

sections.label: What happens without one?
sections.text: Someone with no emergency fund who loses their job usually has to take the first role they find however low the pay, or borrow at very high rates simply to keep going - and a small shock becomes a debt that lasts.

lines: An emergency fund won't make you rich quickly - it stops you becoming poor quickly when things don't go to plan.
